2027-06-01.title: Saint Justin, Martyr
readings: Where are your acts of charity? Where are your righteous deeds?
Their hearts are firm, secure in the Lord
Give to the emperor the things that are the emperor's, and to God the things that are God's
2027-06-01.alt: Memorial. Tuesday of the Ninth Week in Ordinary Time (Year I). The weekday readings are given here; the proper readings of the memorial, 1 Corinthians 1:18–25 (“we proclaim Christ crucified”) and Matthew 5:13–19 (“You are the light of the world”), may be used instead. St Justin, philosopher and martyr, was beheaded in Rome about the year 165. June, the month of the Sacred Heart, begins today. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-06-01.verse: Jesus said to them, “Give to the emperor the things that are the emperor's, and to God the things that are God's.” And they were utterly amazed at him.
theo: For the first days of June the Church reads the Book of Tobit, a family story told among the Jews scattered in exile. Tobit is a good man living in Nineveh, far from Jerusalem. He gives alms, shares his bread with the hungry and, at the risk of his life, buries the bodies of fellow Israelites left in the street. Today's passage begins after one such burial. Tobit sleeps outside by the courtyard wall, and a stupid accident changes his life: “I did not know that there were sparrows on the wall; their fresh droppings fell into my eyes and produced white films.” The physicians only make it worse, “until I became completely blind.” A rich man becomes a dependent. His wife Anna goes out to work: “my wife Anna earned money at women's work.” One day her employers pay her wages and add a young goat as a gift. Tobit hears it bleat and suspects the worst: “Where did you get this goat? It is surely not stolen, is it? Return it to the owners.” He will not believe her. And Anna, hurt, answers with words that cut deep: “Where are your acts of charity? Where are your righteous deeds? These things are known about you!” It is a painfully honest scene. A good man, humiliated by blindness and dependence, becomes suspicious and hard at home. His goodness in the street has not yet reached his own courtyard. The book does not hide this; it lets us see a holy man in his weakness, so that we may see how God will heal him. The Psalm describes the just man as Tobit wanted to be and will become again: “Happy are those who fear the Lord, who greatly delight in his commandments … They are not afraid of evil tidings; their hearts are firm, secure in the Lord.”

In the Gospel the enemies of Jesus come with a trap wrapped in flattery. Pharisees and Herodians, who normally disliked each other, unite: “Teacher, we know that you are sincere, and show deference to no one … Is it lawful to pay taxes to the emperor, or not?” If Jesus says yes, he betrays the people who hate the Roman tax; if he says no, he is a rebel against Rome. Jesus asks for a coin. “Whose head is this, and whose title?” “The emperor's.” Then comes the answer that has echoed through history: “Give to the emperor the things that are the emperor's, and to God the things that are God's.” The coin bears the image of Caesar, so it may go back to Caesar. But the human person bears the image of God (Genesis 1:27), so the whole person belongs to God. Caesar may have taxes; he may not have our worship. St Justin, whom we remember today, lived this answer to the end. Born of pagan parents at Flavia Neapolis in Samaria, he searched for truth among the philosophers, until an old man showed him the prophets and Christ. He wrote to the emperor Antoninus Pius that Christians pay their taxes more readily than anyone, because Christ taught them to give to Caesar what is Caesar's, but that they worship God alone (First Apology 17, in substance). When the prefect Rusticus ordered him to sacrifice to the gods, he refused, and was beheaded with six companions. He gave Caesar his obedience in all things lawful, and gave God his life.
outline: Hold up a coin and ask: whose picture is on this? Then ask: whose picture is on you?
Point 1 · A good man in the dark
Tobit's blindness and his harsh suspicion at home.
Point 2 · The coin and the image
Caesar's image on the coin, God's image on the person.
Point 3 · St Justin, philosopher and martyr
He gave Caesar his taxes and God his whole life.
“Give … to God the things that are God's.”
live: Ask yourself honestly whether the people at home see the same kindness that others see in you outside. Do one act of trust and kindness at home today.
Give God what bears his image (Mark 12:17)
Pay what you owe honestly, and then offer God the first minutes of your day in prayer, because you belong to him.
saints: Born of pagan parents at Flavia Neapolis (Nablus) in Samaria, he studied with Stoic, Peripatetic, Pythagorean and Platonist teachers in search of God. By his own account, an old man he met by the sea told him of the prophets, and “a fire was kindled” in his soul; he became a Christian about 130. Keeping the philosopher's cloak, he taught in Ephesus and Rome. His First Apology, addressed to the emperor Antoninus Pius, gives the earliest full description of the Sunday Eucharist (chapters 65–67); his Dialogue with Trypho is a respectful debate with a Jewish teacher about the Scriptures. He taught that “seeds of the Word” are scattered in all that is true. About 165, under the prefect Junius Rusticus, he and six companions refused to sacrifice to the gods and were beheaded. The Acts of their martyrdom survive. He is the patron of philosophers.
2027-06-01.prayer: O God, who through the folly of the Cross wondrously taught Saint Justin the Martyr the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ, grant us, through his intercession, that, having rejected deception, we may become steadfast in the faith. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Lord, we bear your image; take our whole selves, our minds, our work and our homes. Heal what is blind and hard in us, as you healed Tobit, and make our hearts firm and secure in you. Amen.
altar: St Justin wrote down, about the year 155, what Christians did on Sunday: the reading of the apostles and prophets, the homily, the prayers of the faithful, the bringing of bread and wine, the great thanksgiving to which all answer Amen, and Communion, which he says is not common bread but the flesh and blood of the incarnate Jesus. Eighteen centuries later the shape of our Mass is the same. At this altar we give to God what is God's: ourselves, offered with Christ.

quick: Tobit, a good man, is blinded by an accident and, humiliated, becomes suspicious of his wife Anna, who rebukes him: Where are your acts of charity?
Jesus answers the trap about taxes: Give to the emperor what is the emperor's, and to God what is God's; the coin bears Caesar's image, we bear God's.
St Justin, philosopher and martyr, paid his taxes but would not worship the gods; he was beheaded in Rome about 165.
2027-06-01.action: Do one act of trust and kindness at home today, where it is hardest.
2027-06-01.question: Do the people in my own house see the goodness that others see in me outside?
kidsaint: Justin grew up in a family that did not know Jesus. He loved to ask big questions: who is God? why are we here? He went from teacher to teacher looking for answers. One day an old man by the sea told him to read the prophets of the Bible, and there Justin found Jesus, who is the Truth. Justin became a Christian teacher in Rome. When the judge told him to worship false gods, Justin said no, and he died as a martyr. Lesson: keep asking questions, and look for the answers in Jesus and his Word.

family.explain: Some men tried to trick Jesus with a question about money. Jesus asked for a coin and said: whose face is on it? The emperor's. Then give the emperor his coin. But give God what belongs to God. We do not have the emperor's face on us; we are made in God's image. So we belong to God: our hearts, our hands, our time.
family.intention: We pray for people who have lost their sight, and for families where there is suspicion and quarrelling.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one thing we can give to God this week as a family, because we belong to him?”

illus: A teacher in a Thrissur school once held up a ten-rupee note in a class of thirteen-year-olds and asked: whose picture is this? Gandhiji's, they said. And who owns the note? Whoever has it in his pocket, said one boy. Then she held up a small mirror and passed it round. Whose picture is this? Each child saw his own face. She said: the note goes to whoever has it; but your face is the image of God, and you belong to him wherever you go. One of those children, now a priest, says he still remembers that mirror. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you showed us the coin and the image. We give you ourselves, for we are made in your image. Open our eyes as you opened Tobit's. Amen.
share: Where are your acts of charity? (Tobit 2:14). Has suffering ever made me harsh or suspicious towards the people I love?
Their hearts are firm, secure in the Lord (Psalm 112:7). What bad news am I afraid of, and can I trust it to God?
Give to God the things that are God's (Mark 12:17). What in my life have I kept back from God?
pm.resp: Their hearts are firm, secure in the Lord.
interc: For the Church, that like St Justin she may meet every honest search for truth with patience and courage.
For rulers and governments, that they may serve the common good and respect the conscience of believers.
For the blind and those losing their sight, and for those who care for them.
For families where illness or poverty has brought quarrels and suspicion, that trust may be restored.
For students and teachers of philosophy, through the prayers of St Justin.
pm.close: Father, you made us in your image and redeemed us in your Son. Keep us loyal citizens and faithful children, giving to you what is yours. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today we meet Tobit, a man everyone praised. He gave alms, he fed the hungry, he buried the dead at the risk of his life. And then one night, sleeping by a wall, droppings from some sparrows fell into his eyes. The doctors made it worse, and he became completely blind (Tobit 2:10). In one moment the generous man became the man who must be helped.

Suffering can make us holy, but it can also make us hard. Tobit's wife Anna goes out to work to keep the family. One day she comes home with a young goat, a gift from her employers. Tobit, sitting in his darkness, does not believe her: it is surely stolen, return it. He is ashamed of being poor and dependent, so he suspects the one who is carrying him. And Anna answers: where are your acts of charity? Where are your righteous deeds? (Tobit 2:14). The man who was kind to strangers had become unkind at home. Many of us know that temptation.

In the Gospel Jesus is trapped by a question about taxes. He asks for a coin and says: whose head is this? The emperor's. Then give to the emperor the things that are the emperor's, and to God the things that are God's (Mark 12:17). The coin has Caesar's face, so let it go back to him. But you, my friend, have God's image stamped on you. Caesar may have your coin. God wants you, all of you.

St Justin understood this. He was a philosopher, a seeker of truth, who found Christ. He told the emperor: we Christians pay our taxes more willingly than anyone, because Christ taught us; but we worship God alone. When he was ordered to sacrifice to idols, he refused, and gave his life. Today let us give God what bears his image: our heart, our thoughts, our home, our kindness to those closest to us. And when suffering comes, let us pray with the Psalm that our hearts be firm, secure in the Lord. Amen.
kids: Children, take a coin and look at it. Whose picture is on it? Jesus once held a coin like that and said: give the coin to the king whose picture is on it. Then he said: give to God what belongs to God. And what belongs to God? You do! God made you to look a little like him, inside your heart. So give God your heart, your prayers, your kindness. You are God's treasure!

intro: Theme: “Give … to God the things that are God's.”
A good man humbled in the dark, a coin that bears Caesar's face, and a philosopher who gave God his life.

points.h: A good man in the dark
q: Then she replied to me, “Where are your acts of charity? Where are your righteous deeds? These things are known about you!”
Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ has forgiven you.
points.apply: Notice where suffering or tiredness has made you suspicious or harsh at home, and say one word of trust or thanks to the person you have hurt.

q: So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.
Give to the emperor the things that are the emperor's, and to God the things that are God's.
points.apply: Be an honest citizen this week, in taxes, bills and work; and give God the first place in your day, because you bear his image.

sub: Loyal to the emperor in what is lawful.
q: Happy are those who fear the Lord, who greatly delight in his commandments.
For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
points.apply: Learn one reason for your faith this week, so that you can give an answer with gentleness when someone asks.

concl: Tobit shows us a good man made hard by suffering, whom God will heal; Jesus shows us that the coin belongs to Caesar but the person belongs to God.
St Justin lived both: an honest citizen and a faithful witness, who gave God what bears God's image, his whole life.
2027-06-01.resolve: Each morning this week, before anything else, say: Lord, I am yours; and then be kind at home.
